description: Alumnos de la Universidad Autónoma de Coahuila. Facultad de Sistemas y Facultad de Ciencias Físico-Matemáticas.
summary: The identification of terrestrial analog environments is essential for preparing future missions to the Moon and Mars. This project presents the Planetary Analog Explorer, a web-based platform that integrates a Python analytical engine with an interactive interface to transform satellite imagery from Earth, Mars, and the Moon into actionable scientific insights. The pipeline extracts multidimensional texture features—albedo, multi-scale standard deviation, Sobel gradient, and coherence—modeling each surface patch as a multivariate Gaussian and quantifying similarity via the Bhattacharyya coefficient. A diversity-aware ranking algorithm ensures geographically distinct top-five candidates. Results show that Earth-Mars analogies reach up to 97.33\% similarity, consistently higher than Earth-Moon analogies (up to 76.24\%), due to Mars retaining a more Earth-like geological record. The platform's modular, schema-driven architecture ensures reusability across planetary bodies. Ultimately, the Planetary Analog Explorer provides a scalable, data-driven tool for visually inspecting and quantitatively comparing terrestrial analog candidates for future lunar and Martian missions.
details:
Project Overview

Planetary Analog Explorer is a computational tool designed to identify terrestrial locations whose surface characteristics statistically resemble those found on the Moon and Mars. The project addresses the challenge of identifying potential Earth analogues for future permanent lunar bases and Martian exploration missions.

Rather than relying exclusively on visual comparisons, our team developed a mathematical and computational approach that analyzes georeferenced satellite and planetary imagery in GeoTIFF format. By extracting quantitative surface features and comparing their statistical distributions, the application identifies and ranks terrestrial regions according to their similarity to selected lunar and Martian reference locations.

How Does It Work?

The application consists of two main components: a Python-based analytical backend and an interactive web-based frontend.

The backend processes GeoTIFF datasets obtained from different planetary missions and Earth observation sources. Images are downsampled, divided into square spatial patches, and filtered to eliminate invalid or incomplete regions.

Each patch is characterized using six statistical features that describe its surface properties:

  • Surface albedo.
  • Local standard deviation at three spatial scales.
  • Sobel gradient.
  • Structural coherence.

These features are used to construct multivariate Gaussian distributions, represented by their mean vectors and covariance matrices. The system then applies the Bhattacharyya Coefficient (BC) to quantify the statistical similarity between lunar or Martian reference regions and terrestrial candidates.

The resulting similarity scores are ranked, allowing the system to identify the five most representative terrestrial analogues for each planetary body. Geographic constraints are also incorporated to avoid selecting excessively clustered or redundant locations.

Finally, the results are exported into standardized data formats, including JSON, CSV, PNG, and GeoJSON, for visualization and further analysis.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project provides a quantitative and reproducible methodology for exploring potential terrestrial analogues of extraterrestrial environments.

Its main benefits include:

  • Scientific comparison: Replaces purely subjective visual assessments with measurable statistical features.
  • Exploration planning: Helps identify Earth environments that could serve as comparative references for studying lunar and Martian terrain.
  • Research accessibility: Integrates complex geospatial analysis into an interactive interface that makes the results easier to explore.
  • Extensibility: Supports the incorporation of additional planetary datasets, reference locations, and terrestrial candidates.
  • Reproducibility: Uses standardized geospatial data formats and explicit mathematical methods.

Our intended impact is to provide researchers, students, and planetary science enthusiasts with an accessible tool for investigating similarities between terrestrial and extraterrestrial landscapes. In the long term, this approach could contribute to the preliminary evaluation of analogue environments for planetary exploration research and mission preparation.

Technologies and Tools

The project combines scientific computing, geospatial processing, statistical analysis, and modern web development.

Backend – Python 3

  • Rasterio: GeoTIFF reading, geospatial metadata, and raster processing.
  • NumPy: Numerical operations and statistical calculations.
  • SciPy: Scientific computing and numerical methods.
  • scikit-image: Image processing, including Sobel gradient extraction.
  • Statistical modeling: Multivariate Gaussian distributions, covariance matrices, and the Bhattacharyya Coefficient.
  • Cholesky decomposition: Numerical stability in statistical computations.

Frontend – React and TypeScript

  • React: Interactive user interface.
  • TypeScript: Structured data management and application architecture.
  • React Hooks: Reactive state management and component updates.
  • Leaflet: Interactive planetary map visualization.
  • OpenPlanetaryMap: Planetary basemap tile services.
  • Google Maps: Geographic visualization and satellite imagery references.

Data and Infrastructure

  • GeoTIFF: Georeferenced raster datasets.
  • CSV, JSON, and GeoJSON: Data exchange and results export.
  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS): Planetary data resources.
  • USGS Astrogeology Science Center: Planetary cartographic and geological datasets.
  • GitHub: Source code management and collaboration.

The application was developed using software-based tools and publicly available scientific datasets, without requiring specialized hardware.

Creativity and Innovation

The project's main creative contribution is the integration of statistical pattern recognition with planetary geospatial analysis.

Instead of treating planetary images as simple photographs, the system interprets them as spatial datasets containing measurable surface characteristics. By transforming image regions into multidimensional statistical representations, it becomes possible to compare different planetary environments through a common mathematical framework.

Another innovative aspect is its modular architecture. The analytical backend is independent of the visualization layer, allowing new datasets and planetary bodies to be integrated without redesigning the entire application.

The combination of mathematical modeling, geospatial processing, and interactive planetary visualization transforms a complex scientific comparison process into an accessible exploratory platform.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several scientific, mathematical, and computational factors:

  1. Data compatibility: Different planetary missions provide imagery with different spatial resolutions, projections, and data characteristics. Geospatial preprocessing is therefore essential.
  2. Surface representation: The selected statistical features were designed to capture variations in brightness, local texture, gradients, and spatial structure.
  3. Numerical stability: Covariance matrices may become ill-conditioned, so numerical regularization and Cholesky decomposition are incorporated into the statistical computations.
  4. Geographic distribution: Candidate locations must be geographically distinct to avoid redundant results.
  5. Computational efficiency: Downsampling and patch-based processing reduce the computational requirements of large raster datasets.
  6. Scientific limitations: Similarity in image-derived surface characteristics does not necessarily imply identical geological composition, environmental conditions, or operational suitability.

Final Vision

Planetary Analog Explorer aims to bridge the gap between planetary remote sensing, statistical analysis, and interactive scientific visualization. By identifying measurable similarities between Earth, the Moon, and Mars, the project provides a foundation for further research into terrestrial analogue environments and supports a more quantitative perspective on future planetary exploration.
